Series overview
2
PART ONE · CHAPTERS 1–4
Foundations
Duʿā is not a technique for getting things. It is worship, a statement of tawḥīd, and the clearest confession of our dependence on Allah.
Ch. 1 The basics · Ch. 2 The types of duʿā · Ch. 3 Its excellence and benefits · Ch. 4 The preconditions
What duʿā means
In the language
Duʿāʾ is the verbal noun of daʿā: to call, to summon, to call out. The Qur'an uses it for worship, seeking aid, a request, a call, praise, speech, and a question.
Al-Khaṭṭābī
The servant asks his Lord for help and continued support, shows his neediness, and frees himself from the belief that he has any independent power to change affairs. Pure ʿubūdiyyah.
Ibn al-Qayyim
Asking for what benefits a person, and asking that harm be removed or prevented. Every genuine duʿā runs in one of these two directions.
Jalb al-manfaʿah — bringing benefit: "O Allah, give me X."
Dafʿ al-maḍarrah — removing harm: "O Allah, protect me from X."
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 1
4
Duʿā is worship — the argument
1 · Allah commands it
"Call upon Me, and I will answer you."
2 · Refusal is arrogance
The same verse calls those who will not ask "arrogant toward worship."
3 · So duʿā is worship
The Prophet ﷺ said it outright: "Duʿā is worship." Among the greatest acts of worship.
The consequence that shapes the whole book
You do not get to decide how ṣalāh, fasting or zakāh are performed. Likewise you cannot invent the rules of duʿā. Its manner, etiquette and conditions are derived from the Qur'an and Sunnah — which is why there are chapters on preconditions, etiquette, times, tawassul, and innovations.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 1
5
Every duʿā is a statement of tawḥīd
When you ask Allah you are claiming, implicitly: He exists, He hears me, He knows my situation, He has power over it, He is merciful and generous — and I depend on Him. The servant affirms Allah's perfection and his own weakness in one breath.
Rubūbiyyah
Allah is Creator, Sustainer, Master, Controller. Asking Him for something is admitting He controls it.
Ulūhiyyah
If He alone controls affairs and answers, He alone deserves the worship of being called upon.
Asmāʾ wa Ṣifāt
Each request affirms al-Samīʿ, al-ʿAlīm, al-Raḥīm, al-Qadīr — the Hearing, Knowing, Merciful, Able.
Therefore directing duʿā to a created being is shirk. The question is never whether the intermediary is "holy"; it is who is being invoked as the one able to answer.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 1
6
Two kinds of duʿā, and they are inseparable
Duʿā al-masʾalah — asking
"O Allah, forgive me." "Grant me righteous children." Every such request silently affirms that Allah hears, has power, provides, and responds — so asking contains worship.
Duʿā al-ʿibādah — worship
Alḥamdulillāh, SubḥānAllāh, ṣalāh, fasting, dhikr all contain an implicit appeal. "Lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh" asks for nothing, yet whoever believes it will turn to Allah when he needs something — so worship leads to asking.
"You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help." — the two halves of duʿā
Who makes duʿā
What that looks like
The complete believer
Worships Allah and asks Allah — both, consistently
Worships but will not ask
Thinks asking for needs is beneath spirituality; yet the prophets asked constantly
Asks but does not worship
Recognizes Allah's power only when he wants something — Iblīs asked for respite without submitting
Turns to Allah only in crisis
The pre-Islamic Arabs: sincere at sea, back to idols on land
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 2
7
Everything we ask for falls into four boxes
Existing good → preserve it
"O Allah, preserve my health."
Desired good → obtain it
"O Allah, grant me righteous children."
Existing evil → remove it
"O Allah, cure my illness."
Potential evil → prevent it
"O Allah, protect me from disease."
Preserve good. Obtain good. Remove evil. Prevent evil.
Ask for religious matters (īmān, forgiveness, guidance, Paradise) and worldly ones (health, wealth, children). The believer asks for both; worldly blessings are asked for so they serve the Hereafter.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 2
8
Twenty-five benefits, in nine groups
A · Its rank as worship
Nothing is more noble before Allah than duʿā; the best act, the essence of worship, a sign of īmān.
B · Servitude
Asking is obeying a command, so it is rewarded whatever the outcome. "I am indeed near" (2:186).
C · Allah's Names on display
You ask the Most Generous, so don't be stingy in asking. Duʿā is humility; refusing to ask angers Allah.
D · Salvation
A cause of being saved from the Fire. "The most incapable person is he who does not make duʿā."
E · Qadar
"Nothing repels predestination except duʿā." It can prevent a future calamity and lighten an existing one.
F · Wisdom
The wise person asks the One who controls the result, while still using the means. Allah loves to be asked.
G · The mark of believers
Prophets, angels and the righteous are shown asking. The reward is guaranteed: a sincere duʿā is never wasted.
H · The ummah
A cause of victory alongside action, and the purest form of brotherhood when made for someone absent.
I · The weapon of the weak
The oppressed still have Allah. Duʿā cures body, desire and doubt; it breeds optimism, opens a dialogue with the Creator, and is the easiest worship there is.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 3
9
Two benefits that change how you think
Duʿā and the decree
"Nothing repels predestination except duʿā." Not because Allah learns something new — the duʿā is itself part of the decree. Allah may decree: if My servant asks, this calamity will not occur.
So the believer never reasons "if it's decreed, why ask?" His duʿā may be the very means Allah decreed for preventing it — or for lightening what has already struck.
The reward is guaranteed
Whoever asks Allah receives one of these:
  1. What he asked for
  2. A comparable evil removed from him
  3. A response in another form, by Allah's wisdom
A sincere duʿā is never spiritually wasted. This reframes "answered" and "unanswered" for the rest of the book.
Textual caution the author raises: the hadith "Duʿā is the weapon of the believer…" is fabricated. The meaning is sound — hence the title — but it is not the Prophet's ﷺ words.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 3
10
Ibn al-Qayyim's analogy: duʿā is a weapon
Holding a weapon does not win the battle. Three things decide whether it strikes — and they are the master metaphor of the whole book.
The weapon
Is the duʿā itself correct — sincere, lawful, well-formed?
The hand that wields it
Is the heart present, humble, and certain of a response?
The obstacles
Is anything — ḥarām income, sins, haste — blocking its effect?
These factors raise the likelihood of a response. Allah ultimately answers according to His will.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 4
11
Ten preconditions, in five groups
Group
Conditions
Belief
1 · Know that only Allah responds — tawḥīd before asking. 2 · Ask Allah alone, sincerely: "When you ask, ask Allah; when you seek help, seek help from Allah."
Means
3 · Use legitimate tawassul — Allah's Names, your good deeds, a living righteous person's duʿā, your own humility (detail in Ch. 13).
Attitude
4 · Don't be hasty: "I asked and asked and see nothing" then quitting is the fault, not wanting a quick answer. 5 · Ask only for good. 6 · Ask with good intentions — wealth to support family and give charity. 7 · Bring an attentive heart; mechanical repetition is not duʿā.
Personal state
8 · Pure sustenance — the dusty traveler fed on ḥarām: "how can he be answered?" 9 · Ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ — strongly recommended, not an absolute condition, since authentic duʿās exist without it.
Priorities
10 · Duʿā must not displace something more important: answer the adhān, answer your parent. Jurayj kept praying when his mother called, and her duʿā against him was fulfilled.
Ibn al-Qayyim's seed: a man plants, waters and guards it, then abandons it because it grows slowly. Don't abandon a duʿā because the response is delayed.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 4
12
Part 1 in one chain
Know Allah
Recognize your dependence
Ask Allah
Ask correctly
Persist
Trust the response
The misconception to remove
"Duʿā is a mechanism for getting what I want."
The book's claim
Duʿā is the mechanism through which Allah turns the servant toward Him. The servant starts by wanting the thing and discovers that what he needs is Allah.
Part 1 · Foundations · Ch. 1–4
13
PART TWO · CHAPTERS 5–7
Practice
How the heart and body should approach duʿā, what corrupts the process, and when the Sunnah says the door is widest open.
Ch. 5 Twenty-three etiquettes · Ch. 6 Twenty discouraged acts · Ch. 7 Twenty-seven recommended times
Twenty-three etiquettes, five groups
At the start
  • Praise Allah, then ṣalāh on the Prophet ﷺ
  • Raise the hands
  • Face the qiblah
  • Be in wuḍūʾ
The heart
  • Cry, if it comes
  • Expect the best of Allah
  • Humility and fear
  • Complain only to Allah
  • Pray quietly
  • Admit your sins
  • Implore earnestly
  • Be determined
The wording
  • Fitting Names of Allah
  • Repeat three times
  • Keep it concise
  • Begin with yourself
  • Pray for all Muslims
  • Say Āmīn
A lifestyle
  • At all times, in ease and hardship
  • For all matters, big and small
  • Plentifully — not an emergency button
The occasion
  • In a condition of response (Ch. 8)
  • At a time of response (Ch. 7)
Hands, qiblah and wuḍūʾ are etiquettes, not requirements — you can call on Allah in any state. Tears are a result of sincerity, never a performance.
Part 2 · Practice · Ch. 5
15
Shape the request well
Match the Name to the request
Asking for
Call upon
Forgiveness
al-Tawwāb, al-Ghaffār, al-Ghafūr
Mercy
al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm
Provision
al-Razzāq, al-Ghanī
Pardon (Laylat al-Qadr)
al-ʿAfūw — "You are Pardoning and love to pardon, so pardon me"
The Names are tawqīfī — from revelation, not invented — and they shape the psychology of the duʿā, not just its vocabulary.
Be determined
Never "forgive me if You wish" — you need forgiveness absolutely. Qualify only what you cannot judge: "if this is good for me, grant it."
Be concise
"Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the Fire." One line covers both worlds. Quality is not length.
Start with yourself, then widen
"Forgive me and my parents" — then spouse, children, neighbors, the ummah, the oppressed, the dead.
Part 2 · Practice · Ch. 5
16
Pray quietly, complain only to Allah
"Call upon your Lord with humility and in secret." To companions raising their voices: you are not calling someone deaf or absent.
Ibn Taymiyyah's five wisdoms of quiet duʿā
1 · Strong īmān You believe He hears a whisper.
2 · Sincerity No one else is the audience.
3 · Concentration You withdraw from the room.
4 · Ease The voice does not tire.
5 · Protection Private worship invites no envy.
Yaʿqūb, having lost Yūsuf and then a second son: "I only complain of my grief and sorrow to Allah."
Telling people you are struggling is ordinary human speech. "Why has Allah done this to me?" is a complaint against Allah. Take the deepest pain to the One who can change it.
Part 2 · Practice · Ch. 5
17
Twenty discouraged acts — four kinds of failure
Bad theology
  • Improper or mismatched Names of Allah
  • Not expecting a response — even Iblīs was answered
  • Limiting Allah's mercy
  • Asking only for this world
  • Asking Allah to hasten your punishment
Bad ethics
  • Cursing out of personal anger
  • Asking for evil or severed ties
  • Duʿā against yourself, your children, your wealth
  • Evil intentions behind a lawful wording
  • Transgression — excessive, inappropriate, already-settled requests
Bad psychology
  • Haste, then quitting
  • Wishing for death over hardship
  • "Give me this and I'll never ask again"
  • Experimenting: "let's see if it works"
  • Relying on others to ask for you
Bad etiquette
  • Turning duʿā into poetry
  • Crying out loud in public
  • Over-long congregational duʿā
  • The imam praying only for himself
  • Careless wording of transmitted duʿās
  • Looking upward during ṣalāh
Don't let duʿā become an expression of anger, entitlement, despair, or performance. A parent's angry word against a child can be answered — guard the tongue.
Part 2 · Practice · Ch. 6
18
Twenty-seven times, as a system
Every day
  • Last third of the night — "Who is asking Me, so I can give?"
  • An hour in every night
  • At the adhān, and between adhān and iqāmah
  • In ṣalāh: sujūd (closest to Allah), al-Fātiḥah, before the salām
  • After ṣalāh — the authentic adhkār
  • After wuḍūʾ; on waking at night
  • Before Ẓuhr; when a rooster crows
Every week
  • Friday's hour — after ʿAṣr until Maghrib (the view the author prefers, with Ibn al-Qayyim), or during the khuṭbah
Every year
  • Ramadan, Laylat al-Qadr
  • First ten of Dhul-Ḥijjah; ʿArafah — "the best of all duʿās"
  • When rain falls
Life events
  • Travel
  • Visiting the sick — angels say Āmīn
  • At a deathbed — say only good
  • Severe hardship
  • When armies meet
Hajj and ʿUmrah
  • Before drinking Zamzam
  • Inside the Kaʿbah — and the Ḥijr
  • At Ṣafā and Marwah
  • After the first and second Jamarāt, not the third
The habit the author wants: adhān → respond → ṣalāh on the Prophet ﷺ → ask. Five windows a day, built in. Wake at night? Say the dhikr and ask before touching the phone.
Part 2 · Practice · Ch. 7
19
A duʿā protocol from Chapters 1–7
  1. Turn toward Allah — He alone controls the outcome
  2. Begin with praise
  3. Send ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ
  4. Recognize your need: "I am Your servant"
  1. Admit your shortcomings: "I have wronged myself"
  2. Use the fitting Name of Allah
  3. Make the request, clearly and confidently
  4. Ask for both worlds: "if it is good for my dīn and my ākhirah"
  1. Repeat it three times
  2. Widen it: family, parents, the ummah
  3. Don't become impatient
  4. Come back tomorrow. And the next day.
The goal is not to find the perfect duʿā once. It is to become a person who constantly turns to Allah.
Part 2 · Practice · Ch. 5–7

PART THREE · CHAPTERS 8–10
Diagnostics
Who has a special opening, what a person can do to strengthen his duʿā, and what might be blocking it.
Ch. 8 Twelve conditions of acceptance · Ch. 9 Ten factors that help · Ch. 10 Eight obstacles
Twelve people whose duʿā has special status
Person
Underlying state
The wronged
Deprived of rights — Muslim, sinner or not
The distressed
All apparent means gone; pure ikhlāṣ
After a calamity
Patience, then a replacement (Umm Salamah)
The traveler
Away from home, vulnerable, dependent
Parent for or against a child
A bond of enormous power — mother first
Child for a parent
Gratitude; benefits them after death too
Person
Underlying state
The fasting person
Hunger and obedience — especially before iftar
Reciting Qur'an
Immersed in revelation, angels present
On Hajj, ʿUmrah, jihād
Left home for worship — guests of Allah
For an absent Muslim
Brotherhood with no audience
Constant in dhikr
A tongue already turned to Allah
The just ruler
Justice carried with responsibility
The pattern: the more a person is genuinely dependent on Allah and sincerely turned toward Him, the more the condition cultivates accepted duʿā.
Part 3 · Diagnostics · Ch. 8
22
"Fear the supplication of the oppressed."
To the oppressor: you cannot assume "they aren't religious, so it doesn't count." To the oppressed: Allah knows, even if no one else does, even if justice is slow. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ's duʿā against his false accuser was answered.
"An angel says Āmīn — and to you the same."
Make duʿā for a Muslim in his absence and an angel makes the same duʿā for you. No applause, no post, no recognition: ikhlāṣ, brotherhood, and angelic duʿā in a virtuous cycle.
Part 3 · Diagnostics · Ch. 8
23
Ten factors that strengthen a duʿā
1 · Sincerity Who are you really asking? Ch. 1 in practical form.
2 · Expect the best "I am as My servant thinks of Me." Ask → trust → persist.
3 · Good deeds Not "Allah owes me" — deeds purify the heart that asks.
4 · Parents' rights Uways al-Qarnī: ʿUmar was told to seek his duʿā.
5 · Duʿā in ease "Know Him in ease and He will know you in hardship."
6 · Nawāfil After the obligations are secure, not instead of them.
7 · Repentance Regret, resolve — and restore any rights you took.
8 · Humble state Genuine, like the dusty traveler. Never staged.
9 · Blessed places Mosques, ʿArafah, Minā, the Ḥaram — use the access.
10 · The etiquette Everything in Chapters 4–6, kept.
Instead of asking only "what duʿā should I say?", ask: what kind of person am I becoming while I make this duʿā?
If you only pray when someone is sick, money is short, or an exam is tomorrow, you are training yourself to treat Allah as a crisis manager.
Part 3 · Diagnostics · Ch. 9
24
Eight things that block a duʿā
1 · Ḥarām sustenance
Every outward sign is there — dust, raised hands, "O my Lord!" — but food, drink and clothing are unlawful. "How can he be answered?"
2 · Sins
A film over the heart. The answer is not "I'm sinful, so why ask" but "I'm sinful, so I must repent and ask."
3 · Leaving advice
Abandon commanding good and forbidding evil, and a people may call after punishment comes and not be answered.
4 · Haste
"I asked and asked and see nothing" — then quitting. Distinguish "not yet" from "refused."
5 · Tiring out
Different from haste: slow fatigue. The angels never tire of worship. Ten sincere minutes daily for years beats one night of tears and six months of nothing.
6 · A prohibited request
Answered "as long as he does not ask for sin or the cutting of kinship."
7 · Recklessness
Three cases: a corrupt spouse left unaddressed; a loan given without record or witness; wealth handed to a fool. Tawakkul does not mean dropping the means.
8 · Dropping the etiquette
No sincerity, presence, lawful income or persistence — the weapon itself is weak.
Part 3 · Diagnostics · Ch. 10
25
Three questions to ask about your own duʿā
CHAPTER 8
Am I in a special condition?
Oppressed, traveling, fasting, in distress, at Hajj, praying for someone absent, constant in dhikr? Use it.
CHAPTER 9
What am I doing to strengthen it?
Ikhlāṣ → good deeds → parents → tawbah → nawāfil → humility → etiquette → blessed times and places.
CHAPTER 10
What might be blocking it?
Ḥarām income → sins → neglected duties → impatience → giving up → a forbidden request → recklessness.
Improving the conditions is our responsibility. Dictating the outcome belongs to Allah. Doing all ten things in Chapter 9 is not a contract — which is why the book's next chapter is on the delayed response.
Part 3 · Diagnostics · Ch. 8–10
26
PART FOUR · CHAPTER 11
The Delayed Response
"I asked sincerely, kept the etiquette, and still don't see it." The theological heart of the book: fourteen wisdoms, and what the waiting itself gives you.
Ch. 11 The wisdom behind a delayed response
Fourteen wisdoms behind a delay
  • 1 · Allah is al-Malik — none questions or overturns His decree
  • 2 · Man has no right over his Creator — ask "what does Allah expect of me?", not "what do I have coming?"
  • 3 · The delay is itself a trial — what happens to your īmān while waiting?
  • 4 · Allah is al-Ḥakīm — you see present → wish; He sees past, future, consequences, Hereafter
  • 5 · The thing may carry harm — wealth that would ruin your īmān
  • 6 · His choice is better than yours — more merciful than a mother to her child
  • 7 · You don't know what it sets in motion — Mūsā, al-Khiḍr and the boy
  • 8 · Trials bring you closer — "the greatness of reward is by the severity of the trial"
  • 9 · Something hated may bring good — Sufyān: what you dislike may increase your duʿā
  • 10 · It makes you examine yourself — your intentions, income, worship, sins
  • 11 · It may already have been answered — in a form you cannot see
  • 12 · The duʿā itself may be weak — back to the weapon analogy
  • 13 · Allah's Names are manifested either way — al-Muʿṭī, al-Māniʿ, al-ʿAdl, al-Karīm
  • 14 · It perfects your worship — next slide
"I can't see why Allah would withhold this" never implies "there is no wisdom in it." It only means: I don't know the wisdom.
Part 4 · The delayed response · Ch. 11
28
Four forms a response can take
1
You receive it
The obvious form — and the only one most people count.
2
Something equivalent
Allah gives other than the exact thing requested.
3
An evil is averted
You never learn what calamity your duʿā turned aside.
4
Stored for the Hereafter
A reward worth far more than the thing wanted here.
"Nothing happened" usually means "something happened that I cannot see."
Part 4 · The delayed response · Ch. 11
29
How waiting perfects worship
A · Hope is exercised
"Maybe tomorrow." Every day you keep asking, you keep practicing rajāʾ.
B · You feel your need
Instant answers breed self-sufficiency. Prolonged need teaches "I cannot do this without Allah."
C · Arrogance is checked
Not "I asked and Allah gave" but "I am always the needy servant." (Ibn Taymiyyah)
D · Riḍā becomes real
You don't just say "Allah is Wise"; you show it when His decision contradicts your wish.
E · Humility deepens
Worship is love, fear, hope and humility together; delay draws out all four.
F · The conversation continues
Some servants come to love the calling more than the thing. "I want this" becomes "I want Allah."
G · Shayṭān is fought
"He isn't listening. Why bother?" Answer by returning again. Duʿā is the weapon; seeking refuge is the armor.
A delayed duʿā is a spiritual audit: why am I asking, how do I earn, how sincere is my worship, what needs repentance, have I grown heedless?
Part 4 · The delayed response · Ch. 11
30
Ibn al-Jawzī's five answers to his own soul
"You are being tested."
If there were never obstacles or delays, where would the test be?
"You chase wishes and neglect duties."
Ask what Allah requires of you, not only what you want from Him.
"Perhaps your sins block the path."
Open it with tawbah and taqwā — "whoever fears Allah, He makes a way out" (65:2–3).
"Perhaps it would harm you."
A sick child asks for sweets; whoever cares for him knows better.
"Perhaps it would cost you reward."
What looks like being denied may be an increase in your ultimate good.
Agitation
Reflection
Understanding
Contentment
Joy
Part 4 · The delayed response · Ch. 11
31
THE DEEPEST LESSON OF CHAPTER 11
Sometimes the greatest answer to a duʿā is not the thing you asked for, but the servant Allah makes you become while you are waiting.
Answered ≠ approval. A sinner may be answered, a righteous person delayed. The Prophet ﷺ asked for three things and was given two.
Delayed ≠ abandoned. None of these wisdoms is a reason to stop. Their purpose is the opposite: when the answer is delayed, keep asking.
Part 4 · The delayed response · Ch. 11
32
PART FIVE · CHAPTERS 12–14
Rulings
Four things people wrongly think are forbidden, the six sanctioned means of tawassul, and why destiny makes duʿā necessary rather than pointless.
Ch. 12 Permissible acts · Ch. 13 Tawassul · Ch. 14 Duʿā and destiny
Four rulings people get wrong
Praying for someone without yourself
Permissible. The Prophet ﷺ asked forgiveness for ʿAbdullāh ibn Qays alone. No need to append "and me" every time — duʿā is not inherently self-centered.
Wishing for death
Discouraged for ordinary calamity. In extremity, the prophetic wording delegates the choice: "keep me alive while life is better for me, take me when death is better." Al-Bukhārī used it.
Non-Muslims
Living: ask for their guidance — "O Allah, guide Daws." Died in disbelief: do not ask forgiveness (9:113). Against persistent oppressors: Mūsā and the Prophet ﷺ did; when is for scholars to judge.
Asking a pious person for duʿā
Permissible — which opens the larger question of tawassul in Chapter 13.
The method: don't set the rules of duʿā from intuition. The Sunnah sometimes carves exceptions — look there for the precise boundary.
Part 5 · Rulings · Ch. 12
34
Six sanctioned means of tawassul
Tawassul: seeking a means of nearness to Allah so that a duʿā is accepted — "seek the means of approach to Him" (5:35). It is worship, so it rests on texts, not on logic or desire. The author finds exactly these six.
Means
How it sounds
Evidence in the chapter
1 · Allah's Names and Attributes
"I ask You by every Name which is Yours"
The hadith of the Greatest Name; the duʿā for anxiety
2 · Allah's past favours
"You have never left my duʿā unanswered"
Zakariyyā (Maryam 4) — "You have accustomed me to Your response"
3 · Your own state
"I have been overpowered, so help"
Zakariyyā; Nūḥ (al-Qamar 10); Mūsā in Midyan (al-Qaṣaṣ 24)
4 · Your good deeds
"We have believed, so forgive us"
Āl ʿImrān 16; the three men in the cave — parents, chastity, a worker's wage
5 · The effect of the duʿā
"Cure him, so that he may walk to the prayer"
Duʿā for the sick; Ibrāhīm (Ibrāhīm 37); Mūsā asking for Hārūn (Ṭā Hā 29–35)
6 · A living righteous person's duʿā
"Please make duʿā for us"
Umm al-Dardāʾ and Ṣafwān; ʿUmar and al-ʿAbbās in the drought
Scholars count three, four or seven; the author sees no contradiction, since favours fall under the Names and the effect of a duʿā under good deeds. Anything outside the six is either shirk (directed to another object) or bidʿah (to Allah, by an unsanctioned means).
Part 5 · Rulings · Ch. 13
35
Tawassul and the Prophet ﷺ
Category
What it sounds like
Falls under
Author's ruling
Through your love for him
"Because of my love for Your Prophet, forgive me"
Type 4, good deeds
Allowed
Through his duʿā
Asking him to make duʿā, as the Companions did
Type 6, a living pious person
Allowed in his lifetime; not after his death
Through his status
"I ask You by the status of the Prophet with You"
None of the six
Innovation
The author's case on the third
  • Not in the Qur'an or the authentic Sunnah
  • No authentic report of the first three generations doing it
  • No one loved him more than the Companions, yet in the drought ʿUmar turned to al-ʿAbbās, not to the grave
  • Later scholars' approval does not change what the salaf did not do
Two cautions
Love for the Prophet ﷺ — the best of creation — must not raise him above the rank Allah chose; the author points to what Christians did with ʿĪsā.
Angels convey salāms to him; nothing authentic shows other requests being conveyed.
Other Sunni scholars read these evidences differently; this is the author's position.
Part 5 · Rulings · Ch. 13
36
Asking others for duʿā: allowed, not the default
For personal needs the author holds it is better to ask Allah yourself. Communal needs are different — ʿUmar asked al-ʿAbbās on behalf of all Madinah. Six reasons:
1 · It is your own worship. You pray your own ṣalāh; make your own duʿā.
2 · It shows need to people. A request made to other than Allah can lower you.
3 · No one is as sincere as you. A stranger will not feel your problem.
4 · It breeds reliance. Many stop asking once others are asking for them.
5 · It can harm the one asked. Being sought out can make him feel holy.
6 · The Companions didn't, for worldly needs. They asked for the army at Tabūk, for a mother's guidance.
Mālik ibn Dīnār and Ṭāwūs each told the one who asked them: make duʿā for yourself — Allah is the One who answers the distressed. The mistake is asking someone, then relying on it and never asking yourself.
Part 5 · Rulings · Ch. 13
37
"If it's already written, why ask?"
The objection
If Allah has written it, I'll get it whether I ask or not. If He hasn't, I'll never get it however much I ask. Either way, duʿā changes nothing.
Ibn al-Qayyim's reductio
Then why eat, if being full is destined? Why marry, if a child is destined? The objector already treats food and marriage as real causes; singling out duʿā is inconsistent.
The answer: outcomes are decreed with their means
  • The farmer. Fruit is decreed for the planted seed — and still needs watering and guarding.
  • The illness. That you fall ill is decreed; so is that you will ask for a cure. The duʿā is inside the decree.
  • The sin. Provision can be lost through a sin Allah already knew would happen.
A hardship may be preordained on the condition that no duʿā is made. Ibn Ḥajar's two benefits: the reward of obeying, and the request — which may be conditional on the asking.
The past: accept it as destined — it is known and cannot change.
The future: expect the best and strive, by duʿā and by action — nobody knows what is written for him.

A point to raise in class: the footnote here grades Muʿādh's hadith weak, while Chapter 3 cites the same report as ḥasan through supporting chains. The argument does not depend on it — Salmān's hadith makes the same point.
Part 5 · Rulings · Ch. 14
39
PART SIX · CHAPTERS 15–17
Method
Loose ends from the book, six practices the author classes as innovation, seven narrations he classes as weak — and the one rule behind all of it: a true meaning does not make a report authentic.
Ch. 15 Miscellaneous topics · Ch. 16 Innovations of duʿā · Ch. 17 Weak hadith regarding duʿā
Five things never missing from a duʿā
Guidance
Only Allah guides (18:17); it is built into every recitation of al-Fātiḥah.
Forgiveness
Even the most pious slip; the Prophet ﷺ sought it a hundred times a day.
Paradise, refuge from the Fire
The Bedouin's simple duʿā — approved, because all the longer duʿās circle these two.
ʿĀfiyah
Well-being in both worlds. Al-ʿAbbās asked twice for a comprehensive duʿā and got this both times.
Firmness in faith
His most frequent duʿā: "O Turner of hearts, keep my heart firm on Your religion."
Everything is asked of Allah — "the stores of all things are with Him" (15:21) — but the needs of the religion come before the needs of this life. Mercy, patience and contentment belong on the list too.
Rabīʿah ibn Kaʿb, offered any request, asked only for the Prophet's company in Paradise — and was told to help his request with many prostrations.
Part 6 · Method · Ch. 15
41
Other topics in Chapter 15
Duʿā as proof of transcendence
Hands and hearts rise upward by fiṭrah — even children, even non-Muslims. Al-Hamadhānī asked al-Juwaynī to explain away that pull; he could not. The author argues one side of a long Sunni debate; Ashʿarī and Māturīdī scholars read the texts differently.
Wiping the face after duʿā
Seven narrations, all weak; the dispute is whether together they reach ḥasan. Three positions — recommended, outside ṣalāh only, not recommended. The author prefers not wiping, and condemns neither side.
Every prophet's guaranteed duʿā
Each prophet had one; ours saved his as intercession for his ummah on the Day of Judgement. The guarantee covers that one duʿā — he asked for three things and was given two.
Calling on Allah only in need
Six Qur'anic passages show the same arc: harm strikes, sincere calling, relief, turning away. Aimed at Muslims too. Ibn Taymiyyah: after the answer, keep worshipping sincerely.
The duʿā of Yūnus
"Lā ilāha illā anta, subḥānaka, innī kuntu min al-ẓālimīn" — tawḥīd, praise, confession in one line. "No Muslim says it without Allah answering him."
Three short ones
Be sincere in the funeral duʿā, for the pious and the sinner alike. Even Arabian horses ask each dawn to be beloved to their owners. And a harsh word from the Prophet ﷺ against a Muslim becomes purification — he was sent as a mercy.
Part 6 · Method · Ch. 15
42
Six practices the author classes as innovation
1 · Kissing the thumbs at the adhān
Rests on a fabricated report attributed to Khiḍr through unknown narrators.
2 · Group duʿā after every ṣalāh
No basis, not even a weak hadith. In the drought ʿUmar asked al-ʿAbbās for an individual duʿā; he had people beaten for gathering to pray for him. Allowed where the Sunnah confirms it: the Friday khuṭbah, witr in congregation.
3 · Clasping hands to the chest
The Sunnah is open palms (Ch. 5); the author adds that the posture resembles Christian prayer.
4 · Tawassul by the Prophet's status
Not among the six (Ch. 13). Ibn Taymiyyah: people intercede with each other without permission; no one intercedes with Allah except by His permission.
5 · Specifying the unspecified
Fixing a time, place or wording the Sharīʿah did not: the 12th of Rabīʿ al-Awwal, a set duʿā per ṭawāf round, birthday candles, New Year's wishes. Converse: a duʿā tied to one occasion stays there.
6 · "Aqāmahā Allāhu wa adāmahā"
The reply to "qad qāmat al-ṣalāh" rests on a weak narration in Abū Dāwūd.
Three roots of innovation: weak hadith, whims and desires, and in the worst cases shirk. "Whatever is innovated into the religion is rejected." Congregational duʿā after prayer and tawassul by status are debated among other Sunni scholars; these are the author's positions.

43
Seven narrations that circulate as authentic
Narration (gist)
Grading
Problem with the content
1 · "Duʿā is the weapon of the believer, the pillar of Islam, the light of the heavens and earth"
Fabricated
None — the meaning is sound, hence the title; the attribution is not
2 · Adam asked forgiveness "by the right of Muhammad"; Allah would not have created him otherwise
Fabricated
Contradicts the Qur'an: mankind was created to worship Allah
3 · "When matters overwhelm you, seek help from the people of the graves"
No chain at all
Commands asking the dead — shirk
4 · "Perform tawassul with my status, for my status with Allah is exalted"
No chain at all
Tawassul is worship; it cannot rest on logic or desire
5 · Ibrāhīm in the fire declined to ask, since Allah's knowledge of his state sufficed
No chain; Judaeo-Christian origin
The Qur'an is full of the prophets' duʿās; His knowledge is no excuse not to ask
6 · Walking to the masjid: "by the right that those who ask have over You"
Very weak
No creature has a right over the Creator; answering is a promise, not a debt
7 · In a drought ʿĀʾishah had a window opened above the Prophet's grave, and it rained
Very weak
The window was built long after she died; conflicts with ʿUmar asking al-ʿAbbās
Part 6 · Method · Ch. 17
44
How the author tests a narration
1 · Is there a chain?
Narrations 3, 4 and 5 have no isnād in any book of Sunnah. That ends the discussion.
2 · Is the chain sound?
Narrations 1, 2, 6 and 7 have chains that the hadith specialists graded fabricated or very weak.
3 · Does the content fit?
A fabrication often shows in its wording: it contradicts the Qur'an, commands shirk, gives creation a right over Allah, or clashes with known history.
A true meaning does not make a report authentic. The book's own title is the example: the idea is accepted, the attribution rejected.
Contrast: wiping the face also rests on weak hadith, yet gets latitude because respected scholars judged the reports acceptable combined. These seven get none — fabricated, very weak, or chainless.
Part 6 · Method · Ch. 17
45
The whole book in one progression
Ch. 1–2 · What is it? Worship, and asking Allah
Ch. 3 · Why? The greatest worship; nearness, hope, healing
Ch. 4 · What must be present? Tawḥīd, sincerity, lawful income, presence
Ch. 5 · How? Praise, humility, fitting Names, persistence
Ch. 6 · What to avoid? Transgression, despair, haste, theatre
Ch. 7 · When? Night, sujūd, Friday, Ramadan, ʿArafah, rain
Ch. 8 · Who? The wronged, the traveler, the fasting, the parent
Ch. 9–10 · What helps, what blocks? Deeds and tawbah; ḥarām and haste
Ch. 11 · And if it's delayed? Trust al-Ḥakīm; the waiting is the answer
Ch. 12–17 · Boundaries Rulings, tawassul, destiny, innovation, method
The quality of your duʿā reflects the quality of your relationship with Allah.
